newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi court tells UK nurses to seek reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court tells UK nurses to seek reconciliation.

text.p: The murder trial of two British nurses in Saudi Arabia adjourned for another two weeks on Monday, with the court urging them to seek reconciliation with the victim's family, case lawyers said.

"The court was adjourned until July 7," a spokesman for the International Law Firm (ILF) told Reuters. ILF represents the family of Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford, who was murdered at a medical centre in the eastern Saudi city of Dhahran in December.
"Today's (Monday's) hearing resulted in an additional two-week adjournment during which the defendants have been instructed to seek reconciliation with the Gilford family," an ILF statement said.
It is the third lengthy adjournment since the hearings began on May 19.

The Islamic court in Khobar, near Dhahran, reconvened for its fifth session on Monday after a one-week break. Within that week Gilford's brother and mother offered proof that they were her closest legal heirs, a source close to the case said.

As heirs, the brother Frank and mother Muriel would by Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom have the right to decide for or against the execution of Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, if the court finds them guilty and says capital punishment is the appropriate sentence.
"It's been established that Yvonne's mother and brother were the only immediate surviving blood relatives," the source said.

"(Frank) was granted the power of attorney by his mother," he said. "Frank has an enduring power of attorney, which means that his power of attorney lasts from the time that it is issued until the time the grantor dies...The court understands that."
Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex just days before her 56th birthday.
If Parry and McLauchlan are found guilty of murdering Gilford, they may face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword.
The two have said they were forced into making confessions, which they later revoked. Both women, who have attended every court session, say they are innocent.
The nurses arrived at Monday's hearing from their jail cells in nearby Dammam wearing the long black 'abaya' robes and scarves women must wear in the conservative kingdom.
A source close to the case said a number of other procedural issues remained to be resolved before the trial could continue.

"For example, the court understands that Yvonne's mother is aged, and they want to make sure should she become incapacitated at some future date that the power of attorney will survive or that whatever authority Frank operates on survives," he said.

The victim's 84-year-old mother suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia. Frank, who has spoken out as the legal heir since the murder, has said he favours the death penalty. Neither one has come to Saudi Arabia for the trial, but are represented by their Saudi-based lawyers.

"They (the court) want to make sure that when Frank speaks for the family, he speaks for the family," the source said. "Should there be a death sentence (and Frank approves), they don't want to have the decision crumble on a procedural question or because somebody says 'I didn't really want him to do that.'"
The case stirred up controversy since the women were arrested in December, sparking calls for a more open trial.
Saudi officials, who have barred journalists from the hearings, have repeatedly said the proceedings were fair and that the women had nothing to fear if they are innocent.
